title: RAG Agents in Prod: 10 Lessons We Learned — Douwe Kiela, creator of RAG

summary: Douwe Kiela, CEO of Contextual AI and the researcher who originally pioneered RAG at Meta FAIR, presents lessons learned from deploying enterprise RAG agent systems at Fortune 500 scale. He opens by highlighting the tension between the massive $4.4 trillion AI opportunity cited by McKinsey and the Forbes finding that only 1 in 4 businesses actually derive value from AI. He explains this paradox through Moravec's Paradox from robotics: tasks seeming hard for humans (chess, math) are easy for computers, while seemingly easy tasks (contextualization) remain extremely difficult. This 'context paradox' is the key barrier to enterprise AI ROI. Kiela positions enterprises on a spectrum from convenience (general-purpose assistants) to differentiated value (business transformation), arguing that higher value demands better context handling. He founded Contextual AI two years ago to bridge this gap and shares ten lessons: (1) Language models are only about 20% of a system—think systems, not models; (2) Specialization beats AGI for domain-specific enterprise problems; (3) Enterprise data, even when noisy, is the company's long-term moat—AI must work on it at scale; (4) Pilots are deceptively easy but production is hard, so design for production from day one; (5) Speed and iteration with real users matter more than perfection; (6) Engineers should focus on business value, not mundane tasks like chunking strategies; (7) Make AI easy to consume by integrating into existing workflows, as many deployed systems end up with zero actual users; (8) Design for quick 'wow' moments that evangelize adoption—he shares a Qualcomm example where an engineer found a hidden 7-year-old document; (9) Accuracy is table stakes—beyond a minimum threshold, focus on managing inaccuracy through observability, audit trails, attribution, and postprocessing; (10) Be ambitious—many projects fail from aiming too low (answering vacation-day questions) rather than too high, and the current moment demands transformative goals. He concludes that the context paradox persists but these lessons can turn challenges into opportunities.

sections.title: Introduction and Enterprise AI Opportunity
sections.summary: Kiela introduces himself as CEO of Contextual AI. He highlights the $4.4T AI opportunity (McKinsey) but notes only 1 in 4 businesses get value from AI (Forbes), creating a paradox of high investment vs. low returns.

sections.title: Moravec's Paradox and the Context Paradox
sections.summary: Draws analogy to Moravec's Paradox from robotics: hard things are easy for computers, easy things are hard. Introduces the context paradox—LLMs excel at code and math but struggle with contextualization humans do effortlessly. This is the key to unlocking ROI, moving from convenience to differentiated value.

sections.title: Lesson 1: Systems Not Models
sections.summary: Kiela explains why he founded Contextual AI. First lesson: LLMs are only 20% of a system. A mediocre model with a great RAG pipeline beats a great model with a terrible one. Think systems, not models.

sections.title: Lesson 2: Specialization Over AGI
sections.summary: Enterprise expertise is fuel. Generalist assistants struggle to capture institutional knowledge. Specializing for domain-specific use cases yields much better results than pursuing AGI.

sections.title: Lesson 3: Data Is Your Moat
sections.summary: A company's long-term identity is its data, not its people. Rather than cleaning data first, make AI work on noisy data at scale. Success here creates differentiated value and a defensible moat.

sections.title: Lesson 4: Design for Production, Not Pilots
sections.summary: Pilots are easy with existing frameworks but productionizing at scale—millions of documents, thousands of users, 20,000 use cases, security, compliance—is much harder. Design for production from day one.

sections.title: Lesson 5: Speed Over Perfection
sections.summary: Ship to real users early, even if barely functional, and hill-climb through iteration. Waiting for perfection makes bridging pilot-to-production very difficult.

sections.title: Lesson 6: Don't Waste Engineers on Boring Tasks
sections.summary: Engineers spend too much time on chunking strategies and prompts. Abstract these away with state-of-the-art platforms so engineers focus on delivering business value and differentiation.

sections.title: Lesson 7: Make AI Easy to Consume
sections.summary: Many companies have GenAI in production with near-zero actual usage due to model risk constraints or poor usability. Success requires integrating AI into existing workflows rather than building standalone tools.

sections.title: Lesson 8: Design for Wow Moments and Stickiness
sections.summary: Getting production usage requires stickiness. Design onboarding experiences so users reach a 'wow' moment as quickly as possible. Kiela shares a Qualcomm example: a customer engineer found a hidden 7-year-old document, answering long-standing questions—evangelizing AI adoption through small wins.

sections.title: Lesson 9: Accuracy Is Table Stakes—Manage Inaccuracy
sections.summary: Perfect accuracy is nearly impossible; even 90-95% leaves a gap. Beyond a minimum accuracy threshold, focus on managing inaccuracy through observability, evaluation, audit trails (especially in regulated industries), attribution in RAG systems, and postprocessing to verify claims against evidence.

sections.title: Lesson 10: Be Ambitious and Conclusion
sections.summary: Many AI projects fail not from aiming too high but too low—answering 401k or vacation questions is not real ROI. Aim for transformative problems. Kiela compares the current AI moment to the moon landing and urges the audience to seize the opportunity. He concludes by recapping: build systems not models, specialize for enterprise expertise, be ambitious.
